How this book matches your exam. IB Chemistry (guide first assessed in 2025) is organised into Structure (1–3) and Reactivity (1–3). It is assessed as follows:

  • SL: Paper 1 (1h30: Paper 1A multiple choice and Paper 1B data-based questions), 36%; Paper 2 (1h30), 44%;
  • HL: Paper 1 (2h), 36%; Paper 2 (2h30), 44%;
  • both levels: the scientific investigation (internal assessment), 20%.

This book covers S1.1 Introduction to the particulate nature of matter, S1.2 The nuclear atom and S1.3 Electron configurations, with the HL content marked. The data booklet values used are h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and Nᴀ = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. All calculations were checked with Python. The mark allocations are our own guides, written in the style of IB markschemes.

Unit 1 of 10: Elements, Compounds and Mixtures

Key ideas

  • Elements: substances made of only one type of atom.
  • Compounds: two or more elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio. They have different properties from their elements.
  • Mixtures: substances that are not chemically combined. They can be:
  • homogeneous (uniform composition, for example air or salt water);
  • heterogeneous (non-uniform, for example sand in water).
  • Separation techniques: filtration, crystallisation, distillation, paper chromatography, solvation and recrystallisation.

Worked examples

Example 1: sodium (a reactive metal) and chlorine (a toxic gas) form sodium chloride, a stable white solid. A compound has new properties.

Example 2: to separate salt from sand: dissolve in water, filter, then crystallise the salt from the filtrate.

Example 3: paper chromatography separates the dyes in ink. Rf = the distance moved by the spot ÷ the distance moved by the solvent.

10-mark exam-style question

(a) Distinguish between a compound and a mixture. [3]

(b) Describe how to obtain pure, dry salt crystals from rock salt (salt mixed with sand). [4]

(c) In paper chromatography, a dye moves 3.6 cm while the solvent front moves 9.0 cm. Calculate the Rf value. [3]

Answers:

  • (a) A compound has elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio, with new properties; it can only be separated chemically. A mixture is not chemically combined, has a variable composition, and can be separated physically (A3).
  • (b) Add water and stir to dissolve the salt; filter to remove the sand; heat the filtrate to evaporate some water; leave to crystallise, then dry the crystals (A4).
  • (c) Rf = 3.6 ÷ 9.0 = 0.40 (M1 A2).

Common mistakes

  1. Saying mixtures have a fixed ratio.
  2. Evaporating to dryness (which can decompose some salts).
  3. Giving Rf a unit (it has none).
  4. Mixing up homogeneous and heterogeneous.
  5. Leaving out the filtration step.

Quick recall

  1. What is a compound?
  2. Give an example of a homogeneous mixture.
  3. How is sand removed from salt water?
  4. Does Rf have units?
  5. What is the Rf for 3.6 cm and 9.0 cm?

Answers: 1) Elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio. 2) Air (or salt water). 3) Filtration. 4) No. 5) 0.40.
